title: Inside Brampton's Giant Diwali Mithai Mela Feeding GTA's Sweet Tooth
excerpt: Punjabi by Nature has expanded to 10 Diwali sweet markets across the GTA and Kitchener, stocked over a million boxes and expects about 150,000 visitors at its Gore Road mela alone.
body:
BRAMPTON, Ontario — The mithai mela in a Brampton parking lot was not even the original stop for Balwinder Sandhu and her 20-year-old daughter Saaj. They had come to Punjabi by Nature for pakoras, the Globe and Mail reports, and stayed for the colourful tent, the fairy lights and rows of sweets.

Inside, shoppers with gloves on and boxes in hand worked their way past yellow ladoos and perfectly squared milk cakes. Ms. Sandhu, who has lived in Canada for 33 years, left with two boxes, including dilbahar — a stuffed gulab jamun — and gajrela, a carrot-based sweet, according to the report.

  • Punjabi by Nature is hosting 10 Diwali mithai melas across the GTA and Kitchener this year, up from eight last year, the Globe and Mail reports.
  • The Gore Road mela in Brampton is expected to draw around 150,000 visitors during the week-long festival running until Nov. 8.
  • The company stocked over a million empty boxes and offers more than 200 varieties of sweets at Diwali, compared with roughly 120 the rest of the year.
  • Milk cake is the best seller by a wide margin — the company says it makes 10 to 15 times as much as any other sweet, with trays sometimes emptying within 15 minutes.

Scale is what separates Diwali week from any other week for GTA sweet sellers. Nisarg Barot, marketing manager at Punjabi by Nature, told the Globe that many shoppers stop at the Gore Road mela to buy mithai before heading to prayers, then return for more sweets and gift boxes for family and friends. The site sits near several places of worship, including the Hindu Sabha Mandir and a gurdwara.

Keeping up takes an industrial operation behind the tent. More than 100 workers are involved in making mithai during the festive season, production runs in shifts, and refrigerated trucks deliver fresh stock from a local factory several times a day, the report says. Outside the Gore Road location, chefs squeeze ribbons of batter — flour, water and baking powder — onto a giant pan for fresh jalebi, twist them into spirals and dip them in sugar syrup. Charanjit Singh, one of two chefs making jalebi there, has done the job for five years; by the end of a 9-to-9 shift his wrists ache, and this weekend he expects to go through about 200 kilograms of batter as lines stretch around the plaza.

The range widens sharply for the festival. Alongside staples such as ladoos, milk cakes and jalebi, the melas sell sweets including kaju sunflower, made from cashew paste, and kaju dilkhush. That breadth reflects the wider GTA market: a Toronto guide to Diwali sweets notes that counters across Brampton, Scarborough, Etobicoke and Mississauga fill with kaju katli, rasgullas, barfi, gulab jamuns and gift boxes at this time of year, and advises shoppers to pre-order boxes and platters a few days ahead because popular shops see heavy foot traffic and long lines.

For many shoppers, the purchase is about continuity as much as taste. Shristi Sharma drove in from North York with her husband Himanshu and their nine-year-old son Yuvaan after seeing the mela on social media, the Globe reports. The family moved to Canada about four years ago and spent the first years focused on work and settling in; now she wants her son, who was four and a half when they arrived, to experience more of the traditions she grew up with in India. “Here, you have all those vibes that you miss,” she said.

The mela runs until Nov. 8, and the practical advice from sellers and guides is the same: go early, expect queues at peak hours, and do not leave a specific gift box to the last day — the most popular trays, starting with milk cake, do not stay full for long.
